title: What do you think of Elizabeth Taylor's 1974 movie 'The Driver's Seat'? Daringly off the wall, or a bit desperate?

commenti.body: When I discovered this movie, I watched it six times in a week. It’s a whole mood. I can’t get enough. I’m actually having her coat and blouse made for Halloween — I already have the book she Carrie’s around and I plan to drench myself in white diamonds.

I know it as *Identikit*, and as a fan of films more on the fringe, I think it's fantastic. Taylor puts in an excellent performance, full of nervous energy and confusion that creates tension rooted in worry for her character even as the viewer isn't quite sure exactly what is going on and why she is doing what she's doing.

Elizabeth Taylor had a reported tendency to put Burton’s career before hers when they were married. She was also always artistically ambitious. I think she saw her success as an excuse to try interesting roles.

So yeah, Taylor had immense artistic integrity but also her career was messy in a way that reflected her private life.

I think your comment is very well put.

I think after having been in the studio system for so long she was dying to rebel in all facets of her life and with some things she completely overcorrected and was a mess.

I haven't given *The Driver's Seat* a chance yet but I'm absolutely infatuated with *Suddenly, Last Summer.*  It's got everything the camp fan in me loves from Tennessee Williams having written the play, Gore Vidal having written the script, three powerhouse actors Hepburn, Clift, and Taylor in the leads with Dekker and others supporting.  The subject matter is everything but the kitchen sink.  It truly is an underrated masterpiece.

If you like the camp aspects of 'Suddenly Last Summer' you'll be delighted with 'The Driver's Seat'. What they both share are themes of mental breakdown and sexual violence. Where they differ, is that 'Suddenly Last Summer' is all about repression, whereas 'The Driver's Seat' is more of a surreal dream-like character study of a woman who is deliberately and intentionally self-destructive. 

I don't want to mock it though. Yes, it has its camp side, but it also works as a serious film. If you don't take it too literally (her characters quest in Rome is truly bizarre, and hard to believe something any real woman would want, though apparently Muriel Spark modelled this on a real person she read about in a newspaper), and accept its dream like qualities, it is effective and memorable as a character study.

Elizabeth was very eccentric, she lived in rarefied air. These days, the concept of fame from an early age is conceivable and increasingly attainable- in her day it was a one in a billion shot. This translated to a life apart from most everyone, a wildly different experience- almost alien. Very few of her peers enjoyed the level of success and the options that she did and even fewer took the chances, had the successes, and maintained starpower thereafter. Mickey Rooney? Relegated to comedic relief. Judy Garland? Immense talent, rapid deterioration. The only people who even touched anything resembling her success experience were like...maybe her dear friend Roddy McDowall? But he wasn't anywhere near as famous as her. Not even Shirley Temple would go on to have the kind of career she did. I don't know, I think Elizabeth stands alone. 

So in 1970, at 38 she'd already been working for more than 3 decades. She already won 2 Oscars, she already got her generation's version of "cancelled" a few times over and was still unbelievably famous. At this point, there was nothing necessarily to aspire to because everything she could do was a victory lap, right? So she did wacky shit because she had nothing to lose. It's wasn't desperation so much as boredom, so much as simple fun. 

Elizabeth spent her career playing on god mode for a long time, "Suddenly Last Summer", "Reflections in a Golden Eye", "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof", "BUtterfield 8", pretty much everything she was famous for was wildly provocative. She really DGAF.

I’ve never heard of it, but I like off the wall discoveries, so I’m going to watch it, based on this discussion. 

Not the biggest Taylor fan, but I liked about half a dozen movies she starred in, especially ‘Who’s Afraid’, which is one of my top 50 favourites. 

So thank you.

Umm her career ended in the mid 60s, what are you talking about? I'd say after Virginia Woolf her studio contract was over. She did shitty movies and cameos after. The Drivers Seat was actually a good script and done well, you just need to watch more independent movies.
